sources.title: A meta-analysis of the relation between dream content and memory consolidation
sources.study_design: meta-analysis of studies linking incorporation of pre-sleep learning-task content into dreams with post-sleep memory performance
sources.reported_result: Task-related dreaming was associated with improved memory performance (SMD 0.51, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.74); the NREM subgroup association was statistically significant while the REM subgroup association was not.
limitations: The meta-analysis establishes an association and does not by itself prove that dream incorporation causes memory improvement.
Included studies varied in tasks, dream collection and analytic methods.
Subgroup differences between NREM and REM were based on smaller sets of effects and were described as preliminary.
The findings concern memory-related influences on dream content, not the complete origin of thoughts or subjective awareness.

claims.text: Across 16 included studies reporting 45 effects, task-related dream content was positively associated with post-sleep memory performance.
provenance: peer-reviewed meta-analysis and indexed PubMed bibliographic record
limitations: The association does not establish that dream incorporation caused the memory improvement.
The finding supports a memory-related pathway shaping some dream thought content; it does not explain all thought or phenomenal awareness.
claims.uncertainty: The causal direction, underlying mechanisms and generalisability beyond the studied sleep-learning paradigms remain unresolved.

batch_conclusion.statement: The batch supports a bounded ordinary pathway in which recent learning and memory consolidation are associated with some dream content. It does not resolve the complete causal or phenomenal origin of thought.
